findings.title: Options object silently changes rejectOnClear default to true
findings.cause: When the first argument is an options object, destructuring uses `rejectOnClear = true`, while the public docs and type comments state the default is false.
findings.impact: Callers using `pLimit({concurrency: 1})` get abort rejections from `clearQueue()` even though the documented default behavior is to discard queued work without rejecting returned promises. This can unexpectedly reject `Promise.all()` or error handlers in code that only opted into the options-object form.
findings.evidence: index.js:4-8 initializes object-form `rejectOnClear` to true. index.d.ts:99-105 and readme.md:46-52 document `Default: false`. Runtime probe showed a pending task from `pLimit({concurrency: 1})` rejected with `{state: 'rejected', name: 'AbortError'}` after `clearQueue()`.
findings.reproduction_or_test: node --input-type=module probe: create `const limit = pLimit({concurrency: 1})`, start one running task and one pending task, await one tick, call `limit.clearQueue()`, then race the pending promise; actual result is an AbortError rejection, expected default-false behavior is no rejection.

findings.title: Falsy non-boolean rejectOnClear values bypass validation
findings.cause: The validation condition is gated by the option value itself: `if (rejectOnClear && typeof rejectOnClear !== 'boolean')`, so falsy non-booleans such as `0`, `''`, or `null` are accepted.
findings.impact: The runtime accepts option values that the API and TypeScript surface reject, making JavaScript callers observe inconsistent behavior instead of receiving the documented TypeError for malformed options.
findings.evidence: index.js:12 checks `rejectOnClear` truthiness before checking its type. index.d.ts:99-106 declares `rejectOnClear?: boolean`, and index.test-d.ts:29 expects a string value to be a type error. Runtime probe showed `pLimit({concurrency: 1, rejectOnClear: 0})` was accepted.
findings.reproduction_or_test: node --input-type=module probe: call `pLimit({concurrency: 1, rejectOnClear: 0})`; actual result is accepted, expected result is TypeError `Expected rejectOnClear to be a boolean`.

findings.title: limit.map stops passing indexes for non-array iterables
findings.cause: `map` now checks `Array.isArray(iterable)` and passes `undefined` as the mapper index for every non-array iterable, despite using `Array.from`, whose mapper callback always receives an index.
findings.impact: Set, iterator, and other iterable inputs no longer match the documented `Promise.all(Array.from(iterable, (item, index) => limit(...)))` behavior. Mappers that depend on the index compute wrong results without an error.
findings.evidence: index.js:106-114 passes `iterableIsArray ? index : undefined`. readme.md:78-85 and index.d.ts:30-43 say the mapper receives the item value and index for an iterable. Runtime probe `limit.map(new Set(['a', 'b']), (_value, index) => index)` returned `[undefined, undefined]` (serialized as `[null, null]`).
findings.reproduction_or_test: node --input-type=module probe: `const limit = pLimit(1); console.log(await limit.map(new Set(['a','b']), (_value, index) => index));`; actual indexes are undefined, expected `[0, 1]`.

findings.title: limitFunction drops all call arguments
findings.cause: The returned wrapper is `() => limit(() => function_())`, so it neither declares rest parameters nor forwards them into the wrapped function.
findings.impact: Any function wrapped with `limitFunction` that requires arguments receives `undefined` values, producing incorrect return values or runtime failures while still satisfying the exported TypeScript signature.
findings.evidence: index.js:121-125 returns a zero-argument wrapper. index.d.ts:133-136 declares `limitFunction<Arguments ...>` returns `(...arguments_: Arguments) => Promise<ReturnType>`, and index.test-d.ts:24-26 expects `lf('input')` to type-check. Runtime probe wrapping `(value, suffix) => `${value}-${suffix}` returned `undefined-undefined` for `limited('x', 'y')`.
findings.reproduction_or_test: node --input-type=module probe: `const limited = limitFunction((value, suffix) => `${value}-${suffix}`, {concurrency: 1}); console.log(await limited('x', 'y'));`; actual `undefined-undefined`, expected `x-y`.

findings.title: Number.POSITIVE_INFINITY is rejected as a concurrency limit
findings.cause: Concurrency validation now requires `Number.isInteger(concurrency)` and removed the previous `concurrency === Number.POSITIVE_INFINITY` allowance.
findings.impact: Callers can no longer use `Infinity` to express an effectively unbounded limiter, even though it is a number greater than 1 and the local baseline accepted it. This is a backward-compatible API regression for consumers that disable limiting conditionally.
findings.evidence: index.js:127-130 rejects any non-integer value. `git diff -- index.js` shows the baseline allowed `(Number.isInteger(concurrency) || concurrency === Number.POSITIVE_INFINITY) && concurrency > 0`. Runtime probe `pLimit(Number.POSITIVE_INFINITY)` threw TypeError `Expected concurrency to be a number from 1 and up`.
findings.reproduction_or_test: node --input-type=module probe: call `pLimit(Number.POSITIVE_INFINITY)` and run two no-op tasks; actual result is TypeError, expected acceptance with unbounded execution based on the repo baseline behavior.
